views.name: state_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  state_name,
  population,
  area,
  country_name,
  capital,
  density,
  CASE
    WHEN density IS NOT NULL THEN density
    WHEN population IS NOT NULL AND area IS NOT NULL AND area != 0 THEN (CAST(population AS REAL) / area)
    ELSE NULL
  END AS population_density
FROM state

params.description: Provides one-row-per-state core attributes and computed population density for each state (state_name, population, area, country, capital, and density/population_density).
params.when_to_use: Retrieve basic state-level attributes (name, population, area, country, capital). | Get population density for a state when density is stored or can be computed from population/area. | Compose state-level queries that need a single-row-per-state input (e.g., join to state-level aggregates or to dimensions keyed by state). | Use as the base for reporting where metrics should remain at the state grain before any further aggregation.
params.output_schema: state_name: The state's name — directly from state.state_name (base table column). | population: The state's population count — directly from state.population (base table column). | area: The state's area (same units as stored) — directly from state.area (base table column). | country_name: The name of the country that contains the state — directly from state.country_name (base table column). | capital: The state's capital city name — directly from state.capital (base table column). | density: Precomputed density value if present in the source table — directly from state.density (base table column). | population_density: Population density used by downstream consumers; equals density when density IS NOT NULL, otherwise computed as CAST(population AS REAL) / area when population and area are present and area != 0; NULL if not computable — derived expression (see metrics).
params.grounded_columns: state.state_name | state.population | state.area | state.country_name | state.capital | state.density
params.metric: population_density = CASE WHEN state.density IS NOT NULL THEN state.density WHEN state.population IS NOT NULL AND state.area IS NOT NULL AND state.area != 0 THEN CAST(state.population AS REAL) / state.area ELSE NULL END | density = state.density (pass-through/precomputed) | population = state.population (pass-through) | area = state.area (pass-through)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state-level or 1:1 views/tables on state_name — safe because state_base is one-row-per-state so measures remain unduplicated. Example: join to states_running_lake_area or state_neighbor_counts on state_name. | Do NOT directly join state_base to one-to-many child tables or views (for example city_base, city lists, river_traverse_expanded, lakes_by_state, mountain_stats_by_state, cities_ranked_within_state) without aggregation, because those will multiply state_base rows and thus duplicate state-level measures (population, area, density, population_density). Instead, either: | - Aggregate the child (one-to-many) table to state_name first (e.g., SUM(lake_area) AS total_lake_area BY state_name) and then join to state_base on state_name; or | - Perform the join and then re-aggregate results back to state_name to produce correct state-level measures. | Examples of safe compositions: | - state_base JOIN state_neighbor_counts ON state_base.state_name = state_neighbor_counts.state_name — safe if state_neighbor_counts is one-row-per-state (AGG). | - state_base JOIN state_border_neighbors ON state_base.state_name = state_border_neighbors.state_name — safe only if that sibling view is one-row-per-state (JOIN/normalized) otherwise re-aggregate. | Examples of unsafe direct joins (without re-aggregation): | - state_base JOIN city_base ON state_base.state_name = city_base.state_name — city_base is one-to-many (many cities per state) and will duplicate state-level measures; aggregate city_base to state first (e.g., COUNT(city) BY state_name) before joining. | - state_base JOIN river_traverse_expanded ON state_base.state_name = river_traverse_expanded.state_name — river_traverse_expanded is expanded/joined and may be many rows per state; aggregate first. | Guiding principle: treat state_base as canonical 1 row per state. Only join it directly to other 1:1 or pre-aggregated-per-state datasets on state_name without changing any state_base measures. For any one-to-many child, reduce the child to one row per state (aggregate or window-collapse) before joining.

views.description: Normalized projection of the state table preserving original columns and exposing a derived population_density ratio when density is missing. Use when questions need state-level attributes or a canonical state relation for joins. | Use for: List states with population or density; compute per-state population density; join state attributes to city/river/lake features.

views.name: city_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  city_name,
  population,
  country_name,
  state_name
FROM city

params.description: Provides one-row-per-city basic attributes (city name, state, country, and population) for questions about city-level facts and for composing city-level aggregations.
params.when_to_use: Look up attributes for a specific city (population, state, country). | Aggregate population or count of cities by state or country when the aggregation should treat each city as one row. | Join city-level attributes onto other datasets keyed by city_name and state_name. | Serve as the city-level grain input when building higher-level state- or country-aggregates (must re-aggregate after joining any one-to-many child). | Compose rankings, window functions, or filters that operate at city grain (e.g., top N cities per state).
params.output_schema: city_name: Name of the city as stored in city.city_name (base column city.city_name). | population: Population count for the city as stored in city.population (base column city.population). | country_name: Country name for the city as stored in city.country_name (base column city.country_name). | state_name: State name for the city as stored in city.state_name (base column city.state_name).
params.metric: population = city.population (atomic, stored numeric column; treat as a per-city measure to be summed/aggregated only when explicitly aggregated by caller) | city_count (implicit) = 1 per row at grain [city_name, state_name] (use COUNT(*) on this view to get number of cities)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_base on state_name (JOIN ON city_base.state_name = state_base.state_name) — safe because state_base is one-row-per-state (NORM) and joining will not duplicate city rows; city measures remain one-per-city. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to states_running_lake_area (WIN) on state_name — safe because that view is state-grain/windowed per state and will not duplicate city rows when joined on state_name. | cardinality-UNSAFE (avoid without re-aggregation): do NOT join directly to lakes_by_state (AGG) or mountain_stats_by_state (AGG) or state_neighbor_counts (AGG) if those AGG views produce multiple rows per state (e.g., multiple lake rows) without first ensuring they are one-row-per-state; such joins can multiply city rows and inflate population sums unless you aggregate the AGG view to one row per state before joining. | cardinality-UNSAFE (avoid without re-aggregation): do NOT join directly to river_traverse_expanded or state_with_city_counts or state_highlow_joined if those sibling views are JOIN-expanded or produce multi-row results per state or city (they may duplicate city-level measures). Instead, either aggregate those views to the state level or join on keys that preserve one-to-one relation. | safe pattern for building state aggregates: SELECT state_name, SUM(population) FROM city_base GROUP BY state_name — this re-aggregates city_base measures at state grain and is safe regardless of downstream joins. | when composing with rank/window views (e.g., cities_ranked_within_state), prefer building the ranking from city_base (JOIN on city_name & state_name) or join the ranking back to city_base on the unique city-level key; ensure the ranking view is one-row-per-city to avoid duplication. | key guidance summary: city_base is one-row-per-city (grain: [city_name, state_name]). It is safe to join to any sibling view that is one-row-per-state or one-row-per-city on the matching key(s). Do not join to one-to-many results (multi-row-per-state or expanded traversals) without first aggregating those results to the same grain as city_base or re-aggregating after the join to avoid duplicating population or counts.

views.description: Projection of city rows preserving identifying columns and population measure. Use when questions need city-level attributes or to join cities to their states. | Use for: Top cities by population within a state or country; counts of cities per state; join to state attributes.

views.name: lakes_by_state
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  state_name,
  COUNT(*) AS lake_count,
  SUM(area) AS total_lake_area
FROM lake
GROUP BY state_name

params.description: Per-state aggregate counts and summed lake area: how many lakes are in each state and the total area of those lakes per state.
params.when_to_use: Get the number of lakes and total lake surface area per state (reporting, dashboards). | Join as a state-level lakes metrics source when enriching state dimension records (e.g., show lake_count and total_lake_area alongside state attributes). | Compose higher-level queries that aggregate or compare states by lake metrics (rank states by lake_count or by total_lake_area). | Use as input for calculations that combine state lake metrics with other state-level metrics (e.g., lakes per capita when joined to state population).
params.output_schema: state_name: name of the state - sourced from lake.state_name (grouping key) | lake_count: integer count of lake rows in that state - derived from COUNT(*) over lake rows within each state_name | total_lake_area: numeric sum of the area column for lakes in that state - derived from SUM(lake.area) per state_name
params.metric: lake_count = COUNT(*) -- count of lake rows per lake.state_name as produced by the GROUP BY | total_lake_area = SUM(lake.area) -- sum of lake.area per lake.state_name as produced by the GROUP BY
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_base on state_base.state_name = lakes_by_state.state_name — safe because lakes_by_state has one row per state_name (one-row-per-key), so joining to a 1-row-per-state dimension does not duplicate the lake_count or total_lake_area measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_with_city_counts on state_with_city_counts.state_name = lakes_by_state.state_name — safe only if state_with_city_counts is one-row-per-state; verify that it is aggregated/joined at state granularity before joining, otherwise re-aggregate the result to state level first. | DO NOT join directly to city_base, cities_ranked_within_state, or any other one-to-many child (e.g., city tables) on state_name without re-aggregating, because those joins will multiply lake_count and total_lake_area (one-to-many expansion). If you need city-level detail with lake aggregates, first join lakes_by_state to state_base (1:1), or aggregate the city-side to state level, or recompute aggregates after the join. | DO NOT join directly to river_traverse_expanded or other expanded/joined tables that are one-to-many to state on state_name without re-aggregation, as that will duplicate lake metrics. | If composing with other state-level aggregated views (e.g., state_neighbor_counts, mountain_stats_by_state, states_running_lake_area), ensure those views are also one-row-per-state_name before joining. If they are one-row-per-state, join on state_name is safe and will not duplicate measures. | When a downstream plan needs finer grain (e.g., per-city or per-mountain metrics combined with lake metrics), compute or attach lakes_by_state metrics at state-level and then distribute or join using techniques that avoid multiplying aggregates (e.g., join on state_name and then divide by counts, or recompute aggregates from lake table at the finer grain). | If you need to sum or average lake metrics after joining to a one-to-many table, re-aggregate the composed result: e.g., SELECT s.state_name, SUM(lake_count) ... GROUP BY s.state_name is incorrect; instead combine at state level or recompute aggregates from base lake table to ensure correctness.

views.description: Aggregated measures of lakes per state: count of lakes and total lake area. Use when questions ask about number or total area of lakes per state or need to rank states by lake presence. | Use for: Which states have the most lakes; which states have the largest total lake area; filter states by lake_count or total_lake_area thresholds.

views.name: mountain_stats_by_state
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  state_name,
  COUNT(*) AS mountain_count,
  MAX(mountain_altitude) AS max_mountain_altitude,
  AVG(mountain_altitude) AS avg_mountain_altitude
FROM mountain
GROUP BY state_name

params.description: State-level aggregate counts and altitude statistics for mountains (one row per state).
params.when_to_use: Get how many mountains, the tallest mountain altitude, or the average mountain altitude per state. | Compose state-level mountain metrics into broader state reports (e.g., combine with population or area) without re-aggregating mountain-level data. | Filter or rank states by mountain_count, max_mountain_altitude, or avg_mountain_altitude when presenting state summaries.
params.output_schema: state_name: Name of the state (derived from mountain.state_name). This is the grouping key for the view. | mountain_count: Number of mountain records in that state (derived from COUNT(*) over mountain rows). | max_mountain_altitude: Maximum mountain_altitude among mountains in that state (derived from MAX(mountain.mountain_altitude)). | avg_mountain_altitude: Average mountain_altitude among mountains in that state (derived from AVG(mountain.mountain_altitude)).
params.metric: mountain_count = COUNT(*) over rows in mountain grouped by mountain.state_name | max_mountain_altitude = MAX(mountain.mountain_altitude) grouped by mountain.state_name | avg_mountain_altitude = AVG(mountain.mountain_altitude) grouped by mountain.state_name
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_base on state_base.state_name = mountain_stats_by_state.state_name — safe because state_base is one-row-per-state so joining preserves one row per state and does NOT duplicate the aggregated mountain measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_with_city_counts on state_with_city_counts.state_name = mountain_stats_by_state.state_name — safe if state_with_city_counts is one-row-per-state (it is a JOIN that produces one row per state), so mountain aggregates will not be multiplied. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_neighbor_counts on state_neighbor_counts.state_name = mountain_stats_by_state.state_name — safe when state_neighbor_counts is one-row-per-state, preserving mountain aggregates. | do NOT naively join to city_base (a one-to-many table: state -> cities) on city_base.state_name = mountain_stats_by_state.state_name without re-aggregation, because each city row would multiply the mountain_count, max_mountain_altitude, and avg_mountain_altitude values and produce incorrect totals. If you need city-level details combined with mountain aggregates, either: (a) aggregate city_base to one row per state first (e.g., COUNT(city) per state) and then join, or (b) join first and re-aggregate at state level after the join. | do NOT join to river_traverse_expanded or any expanded/joined view that is one-to-many per state (e.g., river segments, lakes rows, or other granular features) without re-aggregation, because those joins will duplicate this view's measures. Instead aggregate those granular views to one row per state (summing or taking appropriate aggregates) before joining. | When joining to other AGG views that are one-row-per-state (e.g., lakes_by_state, states_running_lake_area if produced one-row-per-state), the join is safe because both sides are at the same state grain; ensure both sides use the same state identifier (state_name) and same state deduplication rules. | If the downstream planner needs to join to a lower-grain table/view (one-to-many), prefer: JOIN (mountain_stats_by_state) to (subquery that aggregates the lower-grain table to state) on state_name; then combine measures at state grain. This prevents accidental multiplication of mountain metrics.

views.description: Per-state aggregated mountain statistics: number of mountains, max altitude, average altitude. Useful for comparing mountainousness across states or filtering states by mountain measures. | Use for: Top states by highest mountain; average mountain altitude by state; states with no mountains (via left join to state).
validated_on: Could you identify which state or states have the highest number of mountains? I need to know the state names and how many mountains they have!

views.name: state_with_city_counts
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  s.state_name,
  s.population,
  s.area,
  s.country_name,
  s.capital,
  COUNT(c.city_name) AS city_count,
  MAX(c.population) AS max_city_population
FROM state s
LEFT JOIN city c ON c.state_name = s.state_name
GROUP BY s.state_name, s.population, s.area, s.country_name, s.capital

params.description: Per-state summary that returns each state's attributes together with the count of cities in that state and the largest city population in that state.
params.when_to_use: Get quick state-level aggregates about number of cities and the largest city population alongside state attributes. | Compose higher-level SQL that needs one-row-per-state metrics (e.g., percent of states with >N cities, join with other state-level aggregates). | Filter or rank states by city_count or max_city_population while retaining state attributes. | Serve as the aggregated input when joining state-level geography/metrics with other one-row-per-state datasets.
params.output_schema: state_name: State name — derived from table state.state_name (GROUP BY key). | population: State population — derived from table state.population (grouped attribute, retained per-state). | area: State area — derived from table state.area (grouped attribute, retained per-state). | country_name: Country name for the state — derived from table state.country_name (grouped attribute, retained per-state). | capital: State capital name — derived from table state.capital (grouped attribute, retained per-state). | city_count: Number of cities in the state — derived metric: COUNT(city.city_name) aggregated over city rows LEFT JOINed to state. | max_city_population: Largest city population in the state — derived metric: MAX(city.population) aggregated over city rows LEFT JOINed to state.
params.grounded_columns: state.state_name | state.population | state.area | state.country_name | state.capital | city.city_name | city.population
params.metric: city_count = COUNT(city.city_name)  -- cardinality-count of city rows per state (NULL-safe via LEFT JOIN; states with zero cities yield 0). | max_city_population = MAX(city.population)  -- maximum of city.population per state (NULL if no cities exist for the state).
params.composition: Join to state_base (NORM) on state_name — safe because state_base is one-row-per-state; joining preserves one-row-per-state and does not duplicate city_count or max_city_population. | Join to state_neighbor_counts (AGG) on state_name — safe because state_neighbor_counts is an aggregation already at the state level (one-row-per-state), so measures are not duplicated. | Join to lakes_by_state (AGG) or mountain_stats_by_state (AGG) on state_name — safe because these are pre-aggregated to one-row-per-state; joining will not multiply city_count/max_city_population. | Join to state_highlow_joined (JOIN) or state_border_neighbors (JOIN) only if those views are known to be one-row-per-state; if they are one-to-many per state, do NOT join them directly because they will multiply this view's per-state measures unless you re-aggregate after the join. | Do NOT join directly to city_base (NORM) or any other one-to-many tables/views keyed by state_name (e.g., city_base, river_traverse_expanded, cities_ranked_within_state, states_running_lake_area if it produces multiple rows per state) without re-aggregation, because those joins will expand the state row into multiple city-level rows and therefore duplicate city_count and max_city_population. If you must bring in city-level detail, join and then re-aggregate (e.g., GROUP BY state_name and recompute COUNT()/MAX()). | When composing with windowed/ranked sibling views (cities_ranked_within_state, states_running_lake_area): be careful — window functions often produce multiple rows per partition. Only join them after reducing to one row per state (for example, filter to rank = 1 or aggregate) to keep measures from being multiplied. | If you need to join to truly many-to-many relations (e.g., a table of state↔feature with multiple feature rows per state), first aggregate that relation to one row per state (summing, counting, or taking MAX as appropriate) and then join on state_name to preserve the correctness of city_count and max_city_population.

views.description: Denormalized relation joining states to the count of cities in each state plus largest city population. Use when questions require state attributes alongside city-derived measures. | Use for: Compare states by number of cities; find states where largest city exceeds a threshold; list state attributes with city counts.

views.name: state_border_neighbors
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  b.state_name,
  b.border,
  s1.population AS population,
  s1.country_name AS country_name,
  s1.capital AS capital,
  s2.population AS neighbor_population,
  s2.country_name AS neighbor_country_name,
  s2.capital AS neighbor_capital
FROM border_info b
LEFT JOIN state s1 ON b.state_name = s1.state_name
LEFT JOIN state s2 ON b.border = s2.state_name

params.description: Provides one row per (state_name, border) pair showing the state's attributes and the neighboring state's attributes (population, country_name, capital).
params.when_to_use: List neighbors of a given state along with both states' populations, countries, and capitals | Compose analyses that compare a state's metrics to each neighboring state's metrics (e.g., population difference per neighbor) | Build downstream joins that need neighbor-level context (e.g., enrich neighbor rows with city or lake aggregates) while preserving the neighbor grain | Filter or aggregate neighbor relationships (e.g., count neighbors by country or compute average neighbor population) when starting from a per-border row
params.output_schema: state_name: the source state's name — derived from border_info.state_name | border: the neighbor state's name (the border) — derived from border_info.border | population: the source state's population — derived from state.population (aliased s1.population) joined on state_name | country_name: the source state's country name — derived from state.country_name (aliased s1.country_name) joined on state_name | capital: the source state's capital — derived from state.capital (aliased s1.capital) joined on state_name | neighbor_population: the neighbor state's population — derived from state.population (aliased s2.population) joined on border | neighbor_country_name: the neighbor state's country name — derived from state.country_name (aliased s2.country_name) joined on border | neighbor_capital: the neighbor state's capital — derived from state.capital (aliased s2.capital) joined on border
params.grounded_columns: border_info.state_name | border_info.border | state.state_name | state.population | state.country_name | state.capital
params.metric: population = s1.population (direct passthrough of state.population for the row's state_name) | neighbor_population = s2.population (direct passthrough of state.population for the row's border) | country_name = s1.country_name (direct passthrough) | neighbor_country_name = s2.country_name (direct passthrough) | capital = s1.capital (direct passthrough) | neighbor_capital = s2.capital (direct passthrough)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to dimension-like single-row-per-<key> views/tables on matching keys — safe because this view is one-row-per-(state_name, border). Examples: |  - Join to state_base on state_name or border: JOIN state_base sb ON state_name = sb.state_name (safe because state_base is one-row-per-state, so it will not duplicate rows). |  - Join to city_base only if city_base is a one-row-per-city dimension and you join on a city key (e.g., capital) with a one-to-one relationship; otherwise it may multiply rows. | Do NOT join without care to one-to-many tables/views that expand per-state (or per-border) records into multiple rows, unless you intend to multiply rows or you re-aggregate after the join. Examples to avoid or re-aggregate first: |  - Do NOT directly join to city tables that list multiple cities per state (one-to-many) on state_name, because each state-border row would be duplicated once per city and state-level measures (population) would be multiplied. |  - Do NOT directly join to lakes_by_state or mountain_stats_by_state (aggregates by state) unless you join on the matching state key and understand their grain: lakes_by_state and mountain_stats_by_state are one-row-per-state aggregates (safe when joined ON state_name or ON border if you intend to attach aggregated metrics for that state). |  - When enriching neighbor rows with many-to-one expansions (for example, joining cities_ranked_within_state which is multi-row per state), either: |      * join on the specific city key (e.g., capital) when that field is unique per city (safe), or |      * aggregate the many-side first to produce a one-row-per-state summary (safe), or |      * accept and handle duplication and then re-aggregate to the desired grain. | Specific safe join patterns: |  - Attach state-level aggregates for the source state: LEFT JOIN lakes_by_state l ON state_name = l.state_name (safe — lakes_by_state is aggregated by state). |  - Attach state-level aggregates for the neighbor: LEFT JOIN mountain_stats_by_state m ON border = m.state_name (safe — one-row-per-state aggregate). |  - Attach counts of neighbors: LEFT JOIN state_neighbor_counts nc ON state_name = nc.state_name (safe — nc is aggregate per state). | Examples of unsafe joins (will duplicate rows unless re-aggregated): |  - JOIN city_base cb ON state_name = cb.state_name (unsafe if city_base contains multiple rows per state). |  - JOIN cities_ranked_within_state cr ON state_name = cr.state_name (unsafe — rank view is multi-row per state). | General rule for planners: this view's measures are row-level attributes (no aggregates). Treat it as a two-dimensional relation with grain (state_name, border). Any join that is one-to-one or many-to-one from this grain to the other side is safe; any join that is one-to-many will multiply rows and therefore requires re-aggregation or a different join key to preserve measure semantics.

views.description: Each row is a bordering pair with attributes for the source state and the neighbor state (denormalized). Useful for questions about neighbor counts, neighbor attributes, or graph analyses when combined with aggregation or recursive CTEs. | Use for: Count neighbors per state; list neighbor attributes; find cross-country borders by comparing country_name and neighbor_country_name.

views.name: river_traverse_expanded
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  r.river_name,
  r.length,
  r.country_name,
  r.traverse,
  s.population AS state_population,
  s.area AS state_area,
  s.country_name AS state_country_name
FROM river r
LEFT JOIN state s ON r.traverse = s.state_name

params.description: Provides river-level records augmented with the state (if any) that the river traverses, exposing river attributes plus the matched state's basic population, area, and country information.
params.when_to_use: Find rivers and see the attributes of the single state they traverse (if any). | Compose river-level reports that need the traversed state's population or area as attributes (e.g., normalize per-capita or per-area calculations at the river grain). | Filter or group rivers by attributes of the traversed state (country, population ranges, area ranges). | Use as a stable, one-row-per-river input when joining additional one-row-per-state dimensions or when aggregating downstream by river_name.
params.output_schema: river_name: the river name; derived from table river.river_name (base column r.river_name). | length: the river length; derived from table river.length (base column r.length). | country_name: the river's country name (as recorded on the river row); derived from table river.country_name (base column r.country_name). | traverse: the state name that the river traverses (may be NULL if no match); derived from table river.traverse (base column r.traverse). | state_population: population of the matched state; derived from table state.population (base column s.population). | state_area: area of the matched state; derived from table state.area (base column s.area). | state_country_name: country name as recorded on the matched state row; derived from table state.country_name (base column s.country_name).
params.grounded_columns: river.river_name | river.length | river.country_name | river.traverse | state.state_name | state.population | state.area | state.country_name
params.metric: state_population = s.population  -- passthrough attribute, not an aggregate (value stored on state table). | state_area = s.area  -- passthrough attribute, not an aggregate (value stored on state table). | length = r.length  -- passthrough attribute, not an aggregate (value stored on river table).
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_base (or any other one-row-per-state view/table) on traverse = state_name — safe because river_traverse_expanded is one-row-per-river and the added side is one-row-per-state, so measures are not duplicated. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_with_city_counts on traverse = state_name — safe if state_with_city_counts is one-row-per-state (it is a JOIN sibling that represents state-level aggregates); this will not duplicate river rows. | DO NOT join this view directly to one-to-many tables/views keyed by state (for example lakes_by_state, mountain_stats_by_state, state_neighbor_counts, or cities_ranked_within_state) without first aggregating those one-to-many sources to one-row-per-state. Reason: those sources have multiple rows per state; joining them directly to river_traverse_expanded (one-row-per-river) will multiply river rows for rivers that map to that state and thus duplicate/overcount any river-level measures. | If you need to combine river_traverse_expanded with an AGG sibling (e.g., lakes_by_state which is aggregated by state), prefer joining on traverse = state_name because lakes_by_state is already aggregated one-row-per-state — this is safe and will not duplicate rows. | When joining to city-level or other many-row-per-state datasets to compute derived metrics (e.g., total cities per traversed state), first aggregate the many-side to one-row-per-state (e.g., COUNT(city) GROUP BY state_name) and then join on traverse = state_name to avoid multiplicative joins. | Joins on river_name to other one-row-per-river sources (if present) are safe because river_traverse_expanded has one row per river_name. | Null-handling: because the view uses LEFT JOIN state s ON r.traverse = s.state_name, rivers with NULL or non-matching traverse will have NULL state_* columns. Downstream joins that assume a matched state should filter out NULL traverse or require an inner join to ensure a state exists.

FROM city

params.description: Ranks cities within each state by population (1 = largest population in that state).
params.when_to_use: Find the largest / top-N / bottom-N cities within each state by population. | Annotate city rows with their within-state population rank for filtering or reporting. | Compose into queries that need a stable one-row-per-city with its within-state rank (e.g., join to state-level aggregates to select top city per state). | Build further aggregations that depend on per-city ranking (e.g., count of cities per rank threshold by state).
params.output_schema: city_name: city name (derived from base table column city.city_name) | population: city population (derived from base table column city.population) | country_name: country name for the city (derived from base table column city.country_name) | state_name: state name the city belongs to (derived from base table column city.state_name) | rank_by_state: integer rank of the city within its state ordered by population desc (derived from window function RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY state_name ORDER BY population DESC) in the view SQL)
params.metric: rank_by_state = RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city.state_name ORDER BY city.population DESC) | population = city.population  -- raw base column (not an aggregate) | country_name = city.country_name  -- raw base column | state_name = city.state_name  -- raw base column
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_base on state_name — safe because state_base is one-row-per-state, so joining cities_ranked_within_state (one-row-per-city) to state_base on city.state_name does NOT duplicate city-level rows or change rank measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_with_city_counts on state_name — safe if you only need to annotate each city with state counts; state_with_city_counts is one-row-per-state so it will not multiply city rows. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_neighbor_counts or other state-level AGG views on state_name — safe for the same reason (they are one-row-per-state). | do NOT join directly to lakes_by_state, mountain_stats_by_state, states_running_lake_area, or other state-level AGG/JOIN views that are one-row-per-state? — actually these are one-row-per-state AGG views and are safe to join on state_name because they will not multiply rows; ensure they are aggregated at state level before joining. | do NOT join to any table or view that is one-to-many relative to city (for example, if there existed a city_events table with multiple events per city) without re-aggregation, because joining such one-to-many detail would multiply this view's city rows and thereby duplicate/ distort any measures that assume one row per city (e.g., rank_by_state). If you need to incorporate one-to-many detail, first aggregate that detail to one row per city (e.g., SUM(event_count) GROUP BY city_name,state_name) and then join. | When composing further window functions that partition by state_name or city_name, be aware that rank_by_state is already a state-partitioned rank. If you plan to compute new ranks over a different ordering or partition, recompute them explicitly rather than relying on rank_by_state to carry through. | If you need state-level aggregations of ranks (e.g., count of cities with rank_by_state = 1), aggregate this view grouped by state_name. Avoid joining back to per-state multi-row datasets unless those datasets are pre-aggregated to one row per state.

views.description: Ranks cities within each state by population (largest = rank 1). Use to implement top-K city queries per state by applying a downstream WHERE rank_by_state <= K. | Use for: Top N cities by population within each state; find the capital's rank within its state by population.

views.name: states_running_lake_area
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  state_name,
  lake_count,
  total_lake_area,
  SUM(COALESCE(total_lake_area,0)) OVER (ORDER BY state_name ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total_lake_area
FROM (
  SELECT state_name, COUNT(*) AS lake_count, SUM(area) AS total_lake_area
  FROM lake
  GROUP BY state_name
) sub

params.description: Per-state aggregates of lake counts and areas plus a state-ordered running total of lake area (one row per state_name).
params.when_to_use: Report total number of lakes and total lake area by state | Produce cumulative/ running-sum of lake area across states ordered by state_name | Join state-level lake metrics as attributes of states (one row per state) | Use as an aggregated building block when composing higher-level state summaries or comparisons
params.output_schema: state_name: state name (GROUP BY key) — sourced from lake.state_name | lake_count: number of lake rows in that state — derived as COUNT(*) over lake grouped by state_name (source: lake.* counted) | total_lake_area: sum of lake.area for that state — derived as SUM(area) over lake grouped by state_name (source: lake.area) | running_total_lake_area: cumulative sum of total_lake_area ordered by state_name — derived as SUM(COALESCE(total_lake_area,0)) OVER (ORDER BY state_name ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
params.metric: lake_count = COUNT(*)  -- aggregated per lake.state_name from lake table | total_lake_area = SUM(area)  -- aggregated per lake.state_name from lake.area | running_total_lake_area = SUM(COALESCE(total_lake_area,0)) OVER (ORDER BY state_name ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)  -- windowed cumulative sum over the per-state total_lake_area
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a state-dimension or one-row-per-state view (for example state_base or state_with_city_counts if it is one row per state) ON state_name — safe because states_running_lake_area has exactly one row per state_name so joining on state_name will not duplicate its aggregated measures. | You may join to other AGG/one-row-per-state sibling views (e.g., lakes_by_state, mountain_stats_by_state, state_neighbor_counts) ON state_name — safe when those siblings are also one row per state (no duplication occurs). | Do NOT directly join states_running_lake_area to any one-to-many table or view (for example raw lake rows, cities, river_traverse_expanded if it expands multiple rows per state, or cities_ranked_within_state) without first aggregating that side to one row per state_name. Joining to a one-to-many will multiply lake_count and total_lake_area because states_running_lake_area is already aggregated at state level. | If you need additional detail from a one-to-many relation (e.g., cities), either: a) aggregate the many-side to one row per state_name before joining, or b) join and then re-aggregate, ensuring you use appropriate SUM(DISTINCT ...) or recompute metrics from base tables to avoid double-counting. | When composing further window functions that rely on running_total_lake_area, preserve ordering semantics: this view's running_total_lake_area is computed with ORDER BY state_name. If you need a different ordering, recompute the windowed cumulative sum after composing and ordering as required.

views.description: Per-state running total of lake area ordered by state_name. Useful for cumulative-distribution style questions across an ordered list of states (alphabetical or other ORDER BY can be replaced downstream). | Use for: Compute cumulative lake area across states ordered by name or other attribute; find percentile cutoffs when combined with total sum.

params.description: Provides one-row-per-state facts combining basic state attributes with precomputed highest/lowest elevation and named points for that state.
params.when_to_use: Fetch descriptive state attributes together with elevation extremes and the corresponding named points (e.g., reporting/state profile) | Compose dashboards that need state-level population, area, capital and summary high/low elevation facts | Join state-level geographic facts to other state-dimension datasets (ensuring cardinality-safe joins) | Serve as a base for additional state-level aggregations or ratios (e.g., population density = population / area)
params.output_schema: state_name: The state's canonical name; derives from table state.state_name (base relation alias s in the view). This is the row grain. | population: The state's population count (numeric/integer) from state.population (s.population). | area: The state's area (e.g., square km) from state.area (s.area). | country_name: The country that contains the state from state.country_name (s.country_name). | capital: The name of the state's capital city from state.capital (s.capital). | highest_elevation: Numeric value of the state's highest elevation from highlow.highest_elevation (h.highest_elevation). | lowest_elevation: Numeric value of the state's lowest elevation from highlow.lowest_elevation (h.lowest_elevation). | highest_point: The name/label of the state's highest point from highlow.highest_point (h.highest_point). | lowest_point: The name/label of the state's lowest point from highlow.lowest_point (h.lowest_point).

params.metric: population = direct column state.population (no aggregation in this view) | area = direct column state.area (no aggregation) | highest_elevation = direct column highlow.highest_elevation (no aggregation; NULL when no matching highlow row) | lowest_elevation = direct column highlow.lowest_elevation (no aggregation; NULL when no matching highlow row) | highest_point = direct column highlow.highest_point (no aggregation; NULL when no matching highlow row) | lowest_point = direct column highlow.lowest_point (no aggregation; NULL when no matching highlow row)

  c.population AS population,
  c.state_name AS state_name,
  -- rank of city population within its state (dense rank descending so ties get same rank)
  (SELECT 1 + COUNT(DISTINCT c2.population)
     FROM city c2
    WHERE c2.state_name = c.state_name
      AND c2.population > c.population
  ) AS state_city_rank,
  -- flag if this city is tied for the maximum population in its state
  CASE WHEN c.population IS NOT NULL
            AND c.population = (
               SELECT MAX(c3.population) FROM city c3 WHERE c3.state_name = c.state_name
            )
       THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_state_max
FROM city c
views.description: Marks cities that are tied for the maximum population within their state using a per-state rank. Exposes the city's population, state, and the rank/flag enabling easy filtering for top-per-state rows.
